headline: Heart Disease Breakthrough: Common Foods Could Treat Half of All Heart Failure Cases
meta_description: Scientists at King's College London discover that urolithin A, found in pomegranates and walnuts, improves heart function by up to 80% in heart failure patient…
summary_short: A natural compound produced after eating pomegranates could revolutionize treatment for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, affecting millions worldwide.
body:
Scientists at King's College London have discovered that urolithin A—a compound naturally produced in the body after consuming pomegranates, walnuts, and certain berries—improves heart function by up to 80%, offering new hope for millions suffering from a particularly difficult-to-treat form of heart failure. The condition, called heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, accounts for roughly half of all heart failure cases. Unlike typical heart failure where the heart weakens, this variant leaves the pump intact but makes the heart stiff and unable to relax properly between beats, causing breathlessness, fatigue, and reduced quality of life. Current treatments struggle because the condition stems from multiple factors including aging, high blood pressure, and diabetes.

In laboratory experiments, researchers found that urolithin A activates a protein called PKGlα, which is crucial for both blood vessel function and heart muscle relaxation. When tested in animal models, the compound increased the heart tissue's ability to relax and significantly reduced harmful scarring, or fibrosis. The findings proved equally promising when urolithin A was tested in engineered human heart tissue created from stem cells—a cutting-edge model that closely mimics actual human heart muscle.

What sets this discovery apart is that urolithin A has already been evaluated in human studies and demonstrates a favorable safety profile, unlike many experimental compounds still in early phases. While researchers caution there isn't yet enough evidence to recommend eating pomegranates as a heart failure treatment, the findings suggest that dietary approaches enhancing urolithin A production may help alleviate the condition. Dr. Joseph Burgoyne of King's College London noted the discovery "raises the exciting possibility of developing new treatments that improve clinical outcomes and quality of life for people living with the condition." The research was funded by the British Heart Foundation.
quick_facts: Urolithin A improves heart function by up to 80% in lab tests
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction accounts for ~50% of all cases
King's College London scientists discovered the compound's cardiac benefits
Found in pomegranates, walnuts, and some berries
Already shown safe in previous human studies
